title: Dove Valley Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dove Valley wells have a 308-foot median depth, with finished well costs modeled at $21,400-$33,600.
h1: Dove Valley Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html: Well records around Dove Valley show a wide range of drilling conditions. The median permitted well is 308 feet deep, but the middle half runs from 86 to 463 feet. Some records extend to 2,485 feet. Reported yields are stronger than many rural Colorado areas, with a median of 15.0 gallons per minute. These figures cover permitted wells within five miles of Dove Valley, including nearby Inverness, Centennial, Grand View Estates, Meridian, Foxfield, and Cherry Creek.

sections.heading: Dove Valley well depth depends on the formation
sections.html:
The typical Dove Valley well is not a shallow well. The median total depth is 308 feet, and 39% of reported wells fall between 300 and 600 feet. Another 26% are under 100 feet, while 14% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest record is 2,485 feet.

This spread matters when you request a drilling bid. A median-depth estimate is useful for budgeting, but it should not be treated as a guaranteed target. Permits name Denver Basin aquifers, Lower Dawson, Denver, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock formations. Local geology can change the depth needed to reach a productive zone, so nearby well records are worth reviewing before buying land.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are generally usable for homes
sections.html:
Of the wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records divide evenly between wells producing 5 to 15 gallons per minute and wells producing more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is encouraging for a typical household, but a pump-yield number is not the same as guaranteed long-term supply. Only 1,230 wells report a pump yield, compared with 2,516 reporting total depth. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage setup, and any history of declining production.

sections.heading: Dove Valley water levels vary widely by record
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 170 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 66 and 471 feet. Only 148 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited sample rather than a complete groundwater map.

Measurements by decade do not show a simple steady drop. The median was 106 feet below surface in the 1970s, 422 feet in the 1980s, and 931 feet in the 2000s. It then measured 270 feet in the 2010s and 135 feet in the 2020s. That uneven pattern may reflect different locations, aquifers, and measurement methods. Get a current measurement for the specific property instead of relying on the decade series alone.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long drilling activity near Dove Valley
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show 4,680 permitted wells within the mapping area. Of those, 2,205 are recorded as constructed. Permitting was most active in the 1980s, with 825 permits, followed by the 1990s with 777 and the 1970s with 768. There were 253 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Hier Drilling Co Inc with Hier, Bruce A., and Hier Drilling Co. with Hier, Peter J. These are record references, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and availability before selecting a driller.

sections.heading: What drilling a Dove Valley well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the median depth of 308 feet, the drilled hole models to about $15,400 to $21,600. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical models to about $21,400 to $33,600.

Those figures are planning numbers, not a fixed proposal. A bid can change with final depth, casing and grout requirements, access, trench length, electrical work, pump size, and water-quality or construction requirements. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing, pump equipment, pressure system, electrical, trenching, testing, and permitting so you can compare bids on the same scope.

sections.heading: Environmental and building checks belong in the offer review
sections.html:
The map shows 154 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles, along with 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 5 historic mine features. That does not prove contamination at a particular lot, but it is a reason to check the property’s well history and order water testing suited to the site. Test before closing if the well is already installed.

Low yield, an unproductive zone, or a dry hole remain possible even where nearby records look favorable. Review the permit, well construction report, casing and grout details, pump equipment, and water-quality results. For a new home, confirm well location, septic setbacks, reserve or replacement area, driveway access, utility routing, and the county’s building requirements before finalizing the lot plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Dove Valley
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby permits rather than using the area median alone. Records from Inverness, Centennial, Grand View Estates, Meridian, Foxfield, and Cherry Creek can provide useful context, but the closest well is not automatically the best comparison. Match aquifer, depth, construction, use, and reported yield where possible.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on reviewing the DWR record, testing the water, and checking the pump and pressure system under load. For vacant land, get a driller’s site review and a written estimate that explains what happens if the first target is not productive. Also verify the intended domestic use, septic design, access for a drill rig, and any augmentation or water-right requirements that apply to the parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dove Valley?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Dove Valley is 308 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 86 to 463 feet. About 39% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, while 14% are at least 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 2,485 feet, showing how much local depth can vary.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dove Valley?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the median depth of 308 feet, drilling the hole models to about $15,400 to $21,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models to about $21,400 to $33,600. Your bid may differ with access, final depth, casing, grout, pump size, and trenching.

faq.q: How much water do Dove Valley wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Half of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and half produce more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, though only 1,230 records include a pump yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Dove Valley?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 154 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 5 historic mine features within about ten miles. Test the specific well before closing or occupying the home, using a laboratory and a panel appropriate to the property’s history.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Dove Valley?
faq.a: The available measurements do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 106 feet in the 1970s, 422 feet in the 1980s, 931 feet in the 2000s, 270 feet in the 2010s, and 135 feet in the 2020s. Only 148 wells report static water level, so check the individual property.
